Definition (stored description): Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of all gas species delivered by injection after plasma breakdown, summed across species.

Documentation (stored): This quantity is the cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of gas introduced into the plasma by injection after plasma breakdown. It combines all injected gas species into one total inventory. The total is defined by $$ N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t) = \sum_s z_s N_s(t) $$ where $N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t)$ is the accumulated equivalent-electron count, $s$ identifies an injected gas species, $N_s(t)$ is the cumulative number of particles of species $s$ delivered since plasma breakdown, and $z_s$ is the equivalent-electron contribution per particle; for an atomic species, $z_s$ is its atomic number, while for a molecule it is the sum of the atomic numbers of its constituent atoms. The quantity applies to all gas species and uses a cumulative sum over the post-breakdown injection history. It excludes gas introduced during prefill before plasma breakdown, instantaneous injection rates, and any single-species inventory such as [accumulated hydrogen count due to gas injection](name:accumulated_hydrogen_count_due_to_gas_injection). It is the post-breakdown counterpart of the prefill inventory [accumulated total prefill gas count](name:accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count); the two quantities differ by the injection phase they accumulate.

Standard name: derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_poloidal_magnetic_flux_coordinate
Definition (stored description): Geometric rate of change of the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface as its signed poloidal flux coordinate varies.

Documentation (stored): This quantity is the geometric derivative of the cumulative volume enclosed by a nested magnetic flux surface with respect to its signed poloidal magnetic-flux coordinate. It is defined by $$ \frac{dV}{d\psi}=\frac{d}{d\psi}V(\psi) $$ where $V(\psi)$ is the volume enclosed by the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, $\psi$ is the signed poloidal magnetic-flux coordinate, and $d/d\psi$ denotes differentiation with respect to that coordinate. The quantity applies separately to each nested closed flux surface. The underlying volume is cumulative from the magnetic axis to the selected surface, so this derivative describes the change in enclosed volume along the flux coordinate rather than a local volume density, a shell volume, or a plasma-population-weighted quantity. It is the derivative of [volume enclosed by a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface); integrating it between two flux-coordinate values gives the difference between the corresponding enclosed volumes. It is distinct from the derivative with respect to the toroidal flux coordinate, which is represented by [derivative of volume with respect to toroidal flux coordinate](name:derivative_of_volume_of_flux_surface_with_respect_to_toroidal_flux_coordinate). Sign convention: Positive when the enclosed volume increases in the direction of increasing signed poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$.

Standard name: difference_of_vacuum_poloidal_current_function_and_initial_vacuum_poloidal_current_function

Definition (stored description): Signed change in the combined external-coil vacuum poloidal current function relative to its initial reference value, representing variation of the toroidal field multiplied by major radius.

Documentation (stored): The quantity is the signed difference between the present and initial values of the vacuum poloidal current function produced by external coil currents. It represents the change in the major-radius-weighted toroidal magnetic field in the axisymmetric current-free vacuum region. Let $F_{\rm vac}$ denote the [vacuum poloidal current function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function). Its change relative to the initial reference state is $$ \Delta F_{\rm vac}=F_{\rm vac}-F_{\rm vac,initial}=R B_{\phi,\rm vac}-R B_{\phi,\rm vac,initial} $$ where $\Delta F_{\rm vac}$ is the signed change, $F_{\rm vac}$ is the present external-coil vacuum poloidal current function, $F_{\rm vac,initial}$ is its value in the initial reference state, $R$ is major radius, and $B_{\phi,\rm vac}$ is the vacuum toroidal magnetic-field component in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $\phi$ is toroidal angle and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity uses the combined vacuum contribution from external coil currents and excludes plasma currents and induced currents in conducting structures. It is a difference from one initial reference value, not the absolute [vacuum poloidal current function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function); within an axisymmetric current-free region, it inherits the parent function's spatial constancy. Sign convention: Positive when the present value of $R B_{\phi,\rm vac}$ exceeds its initial reference value, with $B_{\phi,\rm vac}$ positive in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.
Stored unit: T.m
Assigned physics domain: magnetic_field_systems

Definition (stored description): Effective turn count of a passive loop is the signed number of equivalent windings assigned to a passive conducting loop for electromagnetic coupling. It weights the passive-loop current contribution and may be fractional for equivalent or homogenized loop elements.

Documentation (stored): Effective turn count of a passive loop is the signed number of equivalent windings assigned to a passive conducting loop for electromagnetic coupling. It may be fractional when the represented conductor is an equivalent or homogenized passive-loop element rather than a literal winding. The signed current-turn source strength represented by the passive loop is defined by: $$ \mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{loop}} = N_{\mathrm{eff}} I_{\mathrm{loop}} $$ where $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the signed current-turn source strength of the passive loop, $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the effective turn count of the passive loop, and $I_{\mathrm{loop}}$ is the [current of the passive loop](name:current_of_passive_loop). This quantity applies to the represented passive loop or passive-loop element as one electromagnetic circuit contribution. It has no implicit aggregation over multiple passive loops; if several represented windings or conductor pieces are collapsed into one loop element, their net orientation and coupling are represented by the single algebraic value of $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$. It is distinct from the [current of the passive loop](name:current_of_passive_loop), which is multiplied by $N_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and from the [area of the passive loop](name:area_of_passive_loop), which describes conductor cross section. It is not a turn count for magnetic probes, coil conductor elements, toroidal-field coils, or magnetic field-line winding.

Standard name: initial_polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam
Definition (stored description): Initial ellipticity of a polarimeter beam is the signed minor-to-major semiaxis ratio of its incident electric-field polarization ellipse before plasma entry.

Documentation (stored): Initial ellipticity of a polarimeter beam characterizes the shape and handedness of its incident electric-field polarization ellipse as part of the polarization state before plasma entry. For an incident polarization ellipse, the ellipticity is defined by $$ e_0 = \sigma_0 \frac{b_0}{a_0} $$ where $e_0$ is the initial polarization ellipticity, $a_0$ and $b_0$ are the major and minor semiaxis magnitudes of the incident electric-field polarization ellipse, and $\sigma_0$ is the handedness sign of the incident polarization state. The semiaxes satisfy $0 \le b_0 \le a_0$, so $|e_0| \le 1$; $e_0=0$ corresponds to linear polarization and $|e_0|=1$ to circular polarization. This quantity applies to one incident polarimeter-beam polarization state along a specified line of sight, with no aggregation across distinct beam paths. It is not the full initial polarization vector, does not describe the post-propagation state, and does not encode the ellipse orientation; the [Faraday angle](name:faraday_angle) describes that orientation's rotation. The initial ellipticity is the reference value for plasma-induced changes in ellipticity, including changes caused by Cotton–Mouton birefringence. The [polarization ellipticity of a polarimeter beam](name:polarization_ellipticity_of_polarimeter_beam) describes the corresponding ellipse shape after propagation through magnetized plasma. Sign convention: Positive when, in the right-handed beam-local basis $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{k})$ with $\hat{k}$ along beam propagation, $\hat{e}_1$ along the major semiaxis, and $\hat{e}_2=\hat{k}\times\hat{e}_1$, the electric-field vector rotates from $+\hat{e}_1$ toward $+\hat{e}_2$ as time increases.

Definition (stored description): Launched power of a lower-hybrid antenna is the net RF power coupled into the vacuum vessel toward the plasma, equal to the forward power minus the reflected power at the launching unit. The launching unit may be an antenna module, a single antenna, or the complete antenna set, for which the value is the sum over the constituent units.

Documentation (stored): Launched power of a lower-hybrid antenna is the nonnegative net RF power coupled from the launching structure into the vacuum vessel toward the plasma. It is the net-transfer component of the wave-power budget represented by [power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna). The launched power is defined by the balance: $$ P_\mathrm{launched} = P_\mathrm{forward} - P_\mathrm{reflected} $$ where $P_\mathrm{forward}$ is the [forward power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:forward_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) arriving at the antenna input reference plane from the transmission line, $P_\mathrm{reflected}$ is the [reflected power of a lower-hybrid antenna](name:reflected_power_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) returning toward the transmission line, and $P_\mathrm{launched}$ is the net power entering the vacuum vessel. The launching unit may be an antenna module, a single antenna, or the complete lower-hybrid antenna set. The quantity is extensive, so the launched power of a composite unit is the sum of the launched powers of its constituent units. Launched power excludes the reflected contribution and is distinct from forward power, which includes the portion subsequently reflected. It denotes the net power delivered across the launching aperture into the vessel, not the generator output on the transmission-line side of the reference plane, and it does not by itself resolve where the power is subsequently deposited within the plasma. The [toroidal-mode-resolved launched power](name:launched_power_per_toroidal_mode_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) and the [jointly toroidal- and poloidal-mode-resolved launched power](name:launched_power_per_toroidal_and_poloidal_mode_number_of_lower_hybrid_antenna) are distributions of this same quantity over refractive-index intervals; integrating them over those intervals recovers the launched power of the corresponding antenna row.

Standard name: minimum_over_flux_surface_magnetic_field_magnitude
Definition (stored description): Smallest total magnetic-field strength attained along a specified nested magnetic flux surface, using the field magnitude rather than a signed component.

Documentation (stored): The minimum magnetic-field magnitude is the smallest total field strength attained anywhere on a specified nested magnetic flux surface. It is sign-invariant because it uses the modulus of the magnetic-field vector rather than a signed component. For a surface labeled by the magnetic-flux coordinate $\psi$, the quantity is defined by $$ B_{\min}(\psi) = \min_{\mathbf{x} \in S(\psi)} \left|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})\right| $$ where $B_{\min}(\psi)$ is the minimum magnetic-field magnitude, $\mathbf{x}$ is a position on the surface, $S(\psi)$ is the set of positions belonging to the flux surface labeled by $\psi$, and $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$ is the total magnetic-field vector at that position. The minimum is taken over all positions on each nested magnetic flux surface and includes the complete equilibrium field, including its poloidal and toroidal contributions. It is not a signed component minimum, a flux-surface average, or a minimum taken across multiple flux surfaces. Unlike the [flux-surface-averaged inverse square of magnetic-field magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_inverse_of_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude), this quantity reduces the field magnitude itself by a pointwise minimum rather than averaging its reciprocal square.

Standard name: minimum_safety_factor
Definition (stored description): Signed safety-factor value on the closed magnetic flux surface where the magnitude of field-line winding is smallest, distinct from that surface’s location.

Documentation (stored): The minimum safety factor is the signed field-line winding number evaluated on the nested closed magnetic flux surface where the magnitude of the safety factor is smallest. It represents the extremal value of the safety-factor function within the confined closed-surface domain. The minimizing value is defined by $$ q_{\min} = q(\rho_\ast), \qquad \rho_\ast \in \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{0 \leq \rho \leq 1} |q(\rho)| $$ where $q(\rho)$ is the signed [safety factor](name:safety_factor) on the flux surface labeled by $\rho$, $\rho_\ast$ is the label of a surface at which the magnitude $|q(\rho)|$ is minimized, and $q_{\min}$ is the signed value evaluated there. The label $\rho$ is a monotonic flux-surface coordinate whose endpoints denote the magnetic axis and the last closed flux surface. In flux coordinates $(\rho,\theta,\phi)$, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The extremum is taken over all nested closed magnetic flux surfaces and is neither a flux-surface average nor a sum. The location-defining quantity is separate: poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor identifies the corresponding surface, while this quantity reports only the signed safety factor. It is also distinct from a safety factor evaluated at a prescribed locus, such as the magnetic axis. Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal angle advance of a magnetic field line is in the direction of increasing $\phi$ as the poloidal angle $\theta$ increases.

These coordinates refer to the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The extrema are taken over the entire [radial outline of the plasma boundary](name:radial_outline_of_plasma_boundary), whose total major-radius span is twice this minor radius. This is a single contour-wide size parameter, not a local major-radius coordinate, a flux-surface average, or the distance from the magnetic axis to an individual boundary point. No circular-cross-section assumption is implied. The last closed magnetic flux surface: the outermost flux surface on which field lines close on themselves, bounding the confined plasma. Standard name: spectral_calibration_factor_at_line_of_sight
Definition (stored description): Wavelength-specific interferometric conversion coefficient that converts a signed phase change along a line of sight into electron column density.

Documentation (stored): The spectral calibration factor is the wavelength-specific proportionality that maps an interferometric phase change along one line of sight to the electron column density on that optical path. The conversion is defined by $$ N_{e,\mathrm{line}} = K_{\mathrm{spec}}\,\Delta\varphi $$ where $N_{e,\mathrm{line}}$ is the [line-integrated electron number density](name:line_integrated_electron_number_density), $K_{\mathrm{spec}}$ is this spectral calibration factor, and $\Delta\varphi$ is the signed interferometric phase change. The factor applies to the complete electron-density integral along the associated line of sight and to its corresponding probing wavelength. It represents the electron contribution only and is not a local density, a line-averaged density, or an optical phase itself. Applying this factor produces the line-integrated electron number density; dividing that result by the optical chord length gives [line-averaged electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density). Definition (stored description): Detected photoelectron rate assigned to each wavelength pixel of a spectrometer channel after electronic gain compensation and relative calibration, but before absolute radiometric calibration.

Documentation (stored): This quantity is the spectrally resolved detection rate of photoelectrons produced by a spectrometer channel. It represents the channel response at an individual wavelength pixel rather than an absolutely calibrated optical emission quantity. The rate for wavelength pixel $p$ is defined by $$ R_p = \frac{dN_{\mathrm{pe},p}}{dt} $$ where $R_p$ is the detected photoelectron rate for pixel $p$, $N_{\mathrm{pe},p}$ is the detected photoelectron count assigned to that pixel, and $t$ is time. The quantity applies separately to each wavelength pixel of the spectrometer channel, with electronic gain compensation and relative channel calibration applied. It is not summed over the spectral range, and it is not an absolute radiance or photon-flux measurement. Summing the rates over pixels that contain an identified spectral feature produces the corresponding line-integrated signal, represented by [intensity at spectral line](name:intensity_at_spectral_line). The electrical output [voltage of spectrometer channel](name:voltage_of_spectrometer_channel) is a distinct signal quantity and is not this photoelectron rate.

Definition (stored description): Pressure of thermal electrons at the post-sawtooth-crash locus is the isotropic stress from random electron motion in the plasma edge and scrape-off layer.

It supplies the electron contribution to [thermal plasma pressure](name:thermal_plasma_pressure), which also includes thermal-ion contributions. Standard name: toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field

Definition (stored description): Toroidal magnetic field at the reference major radius generated by currents outside the plasma, with its directional sign retained and plasma-current contributions excluded.

Documentation (stored): Toroidal magnetic field at the reference major radius is the signed toroidal projection of the externally generated [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field). It specifies the nominal vacuum field with plasma-current contributions omitted. The reference value is defined by projection: $$ B_0 = B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}(R_0) = \left.\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\right|_{R=R_0} $$ where $B_0$ is the reference vacuum toroidal field, $B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}$ is the local vacuum toroidal component, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the [vacuum magnetic-field vector](name:vacuum_magnetic_field), and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $Z$ is vertical height, and $R_0$ is the specified reference major radius. This quantity is a component evaluated at the reference radius, not a field magnitude or spatial average. It differs from the total toroidal magnetic field by excluding plasma-generated contributions; the reference radius is not implicitly the magnetic-axis radius. In an axisymmetric current-free region, the [vacuum poloidal current function](name:vacuum_poloidal_current_function) $F_{\mathrm{vac}}$ satisfies $F_{\mathrm{vac}}=R B_{\phi,\mathrm{vac}}=R_0B_0$. This reference field also supplies the field scale for the [toroidal flux coordinate](name:toroidal_flux_coordinate) and associated current-density normalizations. Sign convention: Positive when the vacuum magnetic-field projection points toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counterclockwise when viewed from above.

Standard name: total_external_heating_power

Definition (stored description): Total non-inductive power coupled from external neutral-beam and radio-frequency heating systems to the plasma, summed over auxiliary sources and excluding Ohmic heating.

Documentation (stored): Total external heating power is the aggregate non-inductive power coupled to the plasma by auxiliary heating systems. It includes neutral-beam injection and electron-cyclotron, ion-cyclotron, and lower-hybrid systems, while excluding power associated with Ohmic induction. The defining aggregate relation is $$ P_{\mathrm{ext}} = \sum_{s \in \mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{aux}}} P_s $$ where $P_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is the total external heating power, $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{aux}}$ is the set of included auxiliary heating systems, and $P_s$ is the power coupled to the plasma by auxiliary source $s$. The quantity applies to the whole plasma and is summed over all included auxiliary sources rather than resolved by source, species, or spatial region. It represents external power input that may contribute to both plasma heating and non-inductive current drive; it is distinct from Ohmic heating and from generator power that is not coupled to the plasma. Source-specific contributions include [total power due to electron-cyclotron heating](name:total_power_due_to_electron_cyclotron_heating), [total power due to ion-cyclotron heating](name:total_power_due_to_ion_cyclotron_heating), and power absorbed from a neutral-beam injector, whose aggregate forms contribute to the sum.

Standard name: wave_phase_of_wave_beam
Definition (stored description): Wave phase of the wave beam is the angular argument of the probing-wave envelope; when referenced to launch, it is the envelope phase offset from the launch phase.

Documentation (stored): The wave phase is the angular argument of the complex probing-wave envelope at the wave-beam locus. It is defined relative to a phase origin; when the origin is the launch phase, the value is a signed phase difference rather than an absolute phase with a universal zero. For a launch-referenced value, the phase difference is: $$ \varphi = \varphi_{\mathrm{env}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{launch}} \pmod{2\pi} $$ where $\varphi$ is the launch-referenced phase difference, represented by difference of wave phase and launched wave phase of the wave beam; $\varphi_{\mathrm{env}}$ is the envelope phase at the wave-beam locus; and $\varphi_{\mathrm{launch}}$ is the launched wave phase. The phases use the same phase convention, and $2\pi$ is one full phase revolution. This quantity is the envelope phase, not the carrier oscillation phase. Values differing by an integer number of full revolutions represent the same phase; an unwrapped phase selects a continuous branch, and fringe-jump correction changes that representation without changing the phase modulo one revolution. Sign convention: Positive when the envelope phase at the wave-beam locus advances counterclockwise relative to the launch phase, using the positive-time-exponent phasor convention.

Standard name: accumulated_total_prefill_gas_count
Definition (stored description): Cumulative equivalent-electron inventory of all gas species introduced by injection during the plasma prefill phase, summed over species.

Documentation (stored): This quantity is the total gas inventory accumulated during the plasma prefill phase, expressed as an equivalent-electron count and summed over all injected species. It represents the integrated amount introduced before plasma breakdown, rather than an instantaneous injection rate. The accumulated equivalent-electron count is defined by $$ N_{\mathrm{eq}}(t) = \sum_s \int_{t_0}^{\min(t,t_1)} \dot{N}_{s,\mathrm{eq}}(t')\,dt' $$ where $s$ indexes injected gas species, $\dot{N}_{s,\mathrm{eq}}$ is the equivalent-electron injection rate of species $s$, $t_0$ and $t_1$ delimit the prefill phase, and $t$ is the evaluation time. The sum includes all species; a species-specific quantity such as [accumulated hydrogen prefill count](name:accumulated_hydrogen_prefill_count) is a component of this total. The quantity is distinct from the instantaneous injection rate and from inventories restricted to one species, while [accumulated prefill gas count](name:accumulated_prefill_gas_count) denotes the near-equivalent total inventory.
Assigned physics domain: general
Standard name: accumulated_tritium_prefill_count
Definition (stored description): Tritium prefill count is the amount of tritium introduced by gas injection before plasma breakdown, expressed as one equivalent electron per tritium atom.

Documentation (stored): Tritium prefill count is the accumulated amount of neutral tritium introduced by gas injection during prefill before plasma breakdown, expressed as an equivalent-electron count. Each tritium atom contributes one equivalent electron; a neutral diatomic tritium molecule contributes two. The equivalent-electron count is defined by $$ N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{T,prefill}} = N_{\mathrm{T,prefill}} = \int_{t_0}^{t_{\mathrm{bd}}} \dot{N}_{\mathrm{T}}(t)\,dt $$ where $N_{e,\mathrm{eq}}^{\mathrm{T,prefill}}$ is the tritium equivalent-electron count, $N_{\mathrm{T,prefill}}$ is the accumulated count of injected tritium atoms including molecular constituents, $\dot{N}_{\mathrm{T}}$ is their introduction rate, $t$ is time, $t_0$ is the prefill start time, and $t_{\mathrm{bd}}$ is the plasma-breakdown time. This quantity counts injected tritium, not the retained or ionized tritium inventory. It excludes post-breakdown gas injection, wall recycling, neutral-beam fueling, and pellet fueling. The equivalent-electron convention is an accounting normalization based on neutral atomic composition, not an actual free-electron count. It is the tritium contribution to the [total prefill gas count](name:accumulated_total_prefill_gas_equivalent_electron_count), which sums over all injected species. The [accumulated tritium count due to gas injection](name:accumulated_tritium_count_due_to_gas_injection) instead counts tritium introduced after plasma breakdown.
Assigned physics domain: fueling

Standard name: alpha_angle_of_coil_conductor_element
Definition (stored description): Alpha angle specifying the first inclination of an oblique poloidal-field-coil conductor-element cross-section, measured from the outward major-radius direction.

Documentation (stored): Alpha angle $\alpha$ specifies the inclination of the first cross-sectional axis at a coil conductor element. It applies to the oblique trapezoidal or parallelogram cross-sectional geometry of an active poloidal-field coil. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the angle is defined by $$ \alpha = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\mathbf{a}_1\cdot\hat{Z},\,\mathbf{a}_1\cdot\hat{R}\right) $$ where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The vector $\mathbf{a}_1$ points along the first cross-sectional axis; $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ are the outward major-radius and upward unit vectors, respectively. The function $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the quadrant-resolved angle from the radial and vertical projections. This is an individual-element shape parameter, not an average over the coil. Definition (stored description): Back-surface neutron flux is the local rate of neutron kinetic-energy transfer outward through an object's designated rear surface, per unit actual surface area and time. It is a scalar energy flux, not a neutron count flux, integrated power, or spatial maximum.

Documentation (stored): Back-surface neutron flux is the local rate at which neutron kinetic energy crosses outward through an object's designated rear surface, per unit actual surface area and time. It is a scalar measure of energy transfer, not a neutron count rate. The local energy flux is defined by $$ \Gamma_{n,\mathrm{back}}^{E}(\mathbf r,t) = \frac{\partial^2 E_{n,\mathrm{out}}}{\partial A\,\partial t}(\mathbf r,t) $$ where $\Gamma_{n,\mathrm{back}}^{E}$ is the back-surface neutron energy flux, $n$ identifies the neutron contributions, $\mathbf r$ is position on the back surface, $t$ is time, $E_{n,\mathrm{out}}$ is the cumulative kinetic energy carried by neutrons crossing outward through the surface, and $A$ is actual surface area. The quantity applies locally over the object's designated back surface and aggregates the kinetic-energy contributions of outward-crossing neutrons across their energies. It excludes neutron number flux, neutron production within a volume, energy deposited inside material, power integrated over a surface, and a spatial maximum or average over the surface. Integrating the local flux over a portion of the back surface gives the neutron power crossing outward through that portion. The [maximum of back-surface neutron flux](name:maximum_of_back_surface_neutron_flux) is the greatest local value over the applicable back surface; that maximum is not part of this local quantity.
Stored unit: W.m^-2

Standard name: co_passing_fast_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions

Definition (stored description): Flux-surface-averaged rate of Coulomb-collisional energy transfer per unit volume from co-passing fast particles to fast ions of one specified species and charge state.

Documentation (stored): Co-passing fast-ion charge-state collisional power density is the signed volumetric rate of kinetic-energy transfer from the co-passing part of a fast-particle distribution to fast ions of one specified species and charge state, averaged over a magnetic flux surface. The co-passing restriction selects the donating particles' passing guiding-center orbits, not the recipient ions' orbit class. The defining kinetic-energy moment is $$ P_{i,q}^{\mathrm{co}\to\mathrm{fast}} = \left\langle \int \frac{1}{2}m_i v^2 C_{i,q}^{\mathrm{coll}}\!\left[f_{i,q}^{\mathrm{fast}},f_{\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{fast}}\right] \, d^3v \right\rangle_{\psi} $$ where $P_{i,q}^{\mathrm{co}\to\mathrm{fast}}$ is this power density, $i$ identifies the recipient ion species, $q$ is its specified ionic charge number, $m_i$ is its ion mass, $v$ is the recipient speed, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The distribution $f_{i,q}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ describes the recipient fast ions, while $f_{\mathrm{co}}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ describes the co-passing fast-particle donors. The operator $C_{i,q}^{\mathrm{coll}}$ gives the collisional time derivative of the recipient distribution due to those donors. The brackets denote the volume-shell-weighted magnetic flux-surface average, with $\psi$ labeling the surface. Only the specified recipient species and charge state are included; no recipient-species or charge-state sum is implied. Counter-passing and trapped donors are excluded. Unlike [co-passing thermal-ion charge-state collisional power density](name:co_passing_thermal_power_density_due_to_coulomb_collisions_with_ion_state), this quantity concerns fast rather than thermal recipient ions. It is an energy-exchange rate, not stored kinetic-energy density or volume-integrated power. Summing over all ionic charge states of the same recipient species gives [co-passing fast-ion collisional power density](name:co_passing_fast_ion_power_density_due_to_collisions). Its relationship to the all-orbit parent, [fast-ion charge-state collisional power density](name:fast_ion_charge_state_power_density_due_to_collisions), is an aggregation over co-passing, counter-passing, and trapped donors with the same recipient population and transfer direction. Transfer from a bulk-ion charge state to a fast-particle distribution is a different exchange and must not be substituted for the fast-to-fast transfer defined here. Sign convention: Positive when Coulomb collisions transfer kinetic energy from the co-passing fast-particle distribution to the specified fast-ion charge-state population; negative when the net transfer is reversed.
Stored unit: W.m^-3

Standard name: decay_time_due_to_disruption
Definition (stored description): Characteristic timescale of electric-current decrease during a disruption, defined by a specified linear-threshold or exponential decay convention.

Documentation (stored): This quantity characterizes electric-current decay during a disruption. It encompasses the total plasma current and the current carried by a specified particle population, without imposing a particular current component or decay convention. For a linear threshold convention, the extrapolated full-decay time is defined by: $$ \tau_{\mathrm{lin}}=\frac{t(f_{\mathrm{low}})-t(f_{\mathrm{high}})}{f_{\mathrm{high}}-f_{\mathrm{low}}} $$ where $\tau_{\mathrm{lin}}$ is the linear decay time, $f_{\mathrm{high}}$ and $f_{\mathrm{low}}$ are the upper and lower fractions of a specified reference current magnitude, and $t(f)$ is the time at which the decaying current magnitude reaches fraction $f$ of that reference. An exponential convention instead defines an e-folding time through $I(t)=I_0\exp[-(t-t_0)/\tau_{\mathrm{exp}}]$, where $I(t)$ is the selected current magnitude at time $t$, $I_0$ is its value at reference time $t_0$, and $\tau_{\mathrm{exp}}$ is the exponential decay time. A linear threshold time is not generally equal to an exponential e-folding time. The [plasma-current decay time](name:plasma_decay_time_due_to_disruption) uses the linear construction with upper and lower fractions of 0.8 and 0.2. The [runaway-electron current decay time](name:runaway_electron_decay_time_due_to_disruption) applies to the total toroidal runaway-electron current and permits custom linear, fixed 20–80% linear, or exponential conventions. These specializations characterize different current populations and need not have equal decay times; neither denotes a local current-density decay time or an electron-temperature decay time.
Stored unit: s

Standard name: flux_surface_averaged_time_averaged_normalized_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field_magnitude

Definition (stored description): Flux-surface- and time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude is the amplitude of magnetic fluctuations along the equilibrium field, normalized by a reference field strength, in nonlinear gyrokinetic turbulence.

Documentation (stored): Flux-surface- and time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude is the amplitude of the perturbed magnetic-field component along the local equilibrium field, normalized by a reference field magnitude. It characterizes parallel magnetic-compression fluctuations in nonlinear gyrokinetic turbulence. For each resolved perpendicular spectral wavevector pair, the averaged normalized amplitude is $$\langle f\rangle = \oint f\,dS/|\nabla\psi| \,/\, \oint dS/|\nabla\psi|$$ Here $A$ is the averaged normalized amplitude, $k_x$ and $k_y$ are perpendicular spectral wavevector components, $t$ is time, and $B_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference magnetic-field magnitude used for normalization. The parallel perturbation $\delta B_\parallel$ is the projection of the perturbed [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field) along the local equilibrium-field direction. The overbar denotes a time average, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_\psi$ denotes the [flux-surface average](concept:flux_surface_averaged) on the closed magnetic flux surface labeled by the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) $\psi$. The spectral dependence is associated with $k_x$ and $k_y$: it may be resolved in both components or summed over $k_x$ at fixed $k_y$, retaining the dependence on $k_y$. The modulus is taken before the averages, so this is an average amplitude of the parallel perturbation, not a mean-square or root-mean-square amplitude. It excludes the equilibrium field and perpendicular perturbations. This is the flux-surface-averaged form of the [time-averaged normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude](name:time_averaged_normalized_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field_magnitude). The [normalized perturbed parallel magnetic-field magnitude](name:normalized_perturbed_parallel_magnetic_field_magnitude) is the corresponding local normalized amplitude without these time and flux-surface averages. The flux-surface average is the average of a quantity over a closed magnetic flux surface, weighted by the inverse magnitude of the poloidal flux gradient. The magnitude is the Euclidean norm of a vector quantity, or the modulus of a complex one.

This quantity applies to an individual mode at its rational, or resonant, flux surface at a given instant, including during mode growth and saturation. It is not summed or averaged over modes or over a time interval, and describes rotation rather than mode growth or damping. The island rotation is related to, but is not necessarily equal to, the local bulk-plasma rotation at that surface. Definition (stored description): Isotropic kinetic pressure of the ion population at a plasma location, summed over all charge states and spanning thermal and non-thermal (fast-ion) contributions.

Documentation (stored): Ion pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure of the ion fluid, defined through the second velocity moment of the ion distribution function. It encompasses both the bulk thermal contribution from ions in local thermodynamic equilibrium and the non-thermal fast-ion contribution from suprathermal particles produced by auxiliary heating. The quantity is summed over all ion charge states present in the plasma. The total ion pressure decomposes as: $$ p_i = p_{i,\mathrm{thermal}} + p_{i,\mathrm{fast}} $$ where $p_{i,\mathrm{thermal}}$ is the isotropic thermal pressure from random ion motion and $p_{i,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the contribution from the suprathermal ion distribution, both summed over all charge states. The thermal component, [thermal_ion_pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure), is inferred from ion temperature and density profiles measured by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or Thomson scattering. The combined quantity total_ion_pressure enters radial force balance, beta calculations, and pressure-driven instability analysis; the fast-ion fraction can be dominant during high-power neutral beam or ion cyclotron heating. Sign convention: Positive when the ion population contributes outward pressure force on a bounding surface element, which holds for any plasma with finite ion thermal energy or non-thermal fast-ion content.

Definition (stored description): Minimum gas flow is the smallest pressure-volume gas throughput that a gas injection valve can reliably deliver, defining the lower bound of its controllable range.

Documentation (stored): Minimum gas flow is the lower reliable operating limit of the pressure-volume throughput delivered by a gas injection valve. It identifies the smallest controllable value of the aggregate gas stream throughput, rather than a molecular-species flow or particle-number rate. The pressure-volume throughput represented by this quantity is defined as $$ Q_g = p_g \frac{dV_g}{dt} $$ where $Q_g$ is gas pressure-volume throughput, $p_g$ is gas pressure at the flow boundary, $V_g$ is the volume of gas crossing that boundary, and $t$ is time. This quantity applies to the aggregate gas stream delivered through an injection system across a defined flow boundary. The stream is not restricted to a particular molecular species or charge state, and this quantity is distinct from mass flow and particle-number rate. Its defining distinction is the lower reliable operating bound, rather than an unrestricted instantaneous throughput. The gas flow quantity defines the same pressure-volume throughput without imposing a lower-limit condition; minimum gas flow is its lower reliable operating bound. Conversely, [maximum gas flow](name:maximum_gas_flow) is the upper reliable operating bound, so the two quantities delimit the controllable range rather than represent different throughput definitions.

Standard name: parallel_fast_ion_charge_state_pressure

Definition (stored description): Pressure of suprathermal ions of one species and charge state arising from velocity fluctuations along the local magnetic field, with the population's mean flow removed.

Documentation (stored): Pressure of suprathermal ions of one specified species and charge state is the field-aligned normal stress from velocity fluctuations about that population's mean flow. It is one of the two independent components of the gyrotropic fast-ion pressure tensor, the other being perpendicular to the local magnetic field. The parallel pressure is defined by the field-aligned central second moment of the fast-ion distribution: $$ p_{s,c,\parallel}^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x}) = m_s \int \left((\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{s,c})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{b}}\right)^2 f_{s,c}^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v $$ where $p_{s,c,\parallel}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the parallel fast-ion pressure for species $s$ and charge state $c$, $\mathbf{x}$ is spatial position, $m_s$ is the ion mass, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $\mathbf{u}_{s,c}$ is the mean velocity of that fast-ion population, $f_{s,c}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is its velocity distribution function, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. The unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ follows the local magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$. This quantity includes only the specified suprathermal ion species and charge state, with no sum over species or charge states. It excludes thermal-ion and electron pressures, the perpendicular pressure component, and stress from the population's mean directed motion. It is not the isotropic trace pressure and does not require an isotropic distribution. It is the parallel component of [fast-ion charge-state pressure](name:fast_ion_charge_state_pressure). Adding the contributions from all charge states of a fixed ion species gives its [parallel fast-ion pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_pressure); this aggregation is an additive sum, not a density-weighted mean.

Standard name: particle_energy

Definition (stored description): Particle energy is the energy associated with particle motion, inherited by specialized forms that are either a kinetic-energy-like coordinate of a velocity-space distribution or the kinetic energy of a particle population.

Documentation (stored): Particle energy is the energy associated with the kinetic motion of particles. It is the general quantity inherited by its specialized forms, which differ in whether the energy is a coordinate attached to individual particle motion or a total carried by a particle population. For a single particle of mass $m$ moving nonrelativistically with velocity $\mathbf{v}$, the underlying kinetic energy is: $$ W = \frac{1}{2}m|\mathbf{v}|^2 $$ where $W$ is the particle kinetic energy, $m$ is the particle mass, and $\mathbf{v}$ is the particle velocity. Specialized forms use this energy, or an equivalent velocity-space weighting, in different roles. The general quantity does not select a species, particle population, spatial region, velocity component, or aggregation convention. It is therefore not inherently a population-integrated total, not restricted to suprathermal particles, and not inherently a gyrokinetic coordinate. It is distinct from potential energy, thermal energy defined by a temperature, and field energy. The specialized forms each fix part of this freedom. [Effective particle energy](name:effective_particle_energy) is a species-dependent, kinetic-energy-like coordinate that parameterizes a particle velocity-space distribution in gyrokinetic theory; it is a coordinate, not a population-integrated total. [Fast-particle energy](name:fast_particle_energy) is the total kinetic energy stored in a specified suprathermal population, integrated over the plasma volume and including motion parallel and perpendicular to the local magnetic field. The first fixes a species-dependent distribution coordinate, while the second fixes a population and a volume-integrated total.
Stored unit: J
Standard name: per_toroidal_mode_mhd_frequency
Definition (stored description): Frequency of oscillation of a linear magnetohydrodynamic mode, equal to the real part of its complex cyclic eigenfrequency.

Documentation (stored): Frequency of a linear magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) mode specifies the oscillation rate of its perturbation. It applies to one mode with a specified toroidal Fourier harmonic, without summing or averaging over modes. It is defined by $$ f = \frac{\operatorname{Re}\omega}{2\pi} $$ where $f$ is the cyclic mode frequency, $\omega$ is the complex angular eigenfrequency, and $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real part. For temporal dependence $e^{-i\omega t}$, $t$ is time and $i$ is the imaginary unit. Writing $\omega = 2\pi f + i\gamma$ defines $\gamma$ as the exponential amplitude growth rate: positive values give growth and negative values give damping. The frequency describes oscillation, not exponential growth or damping, and differs from the real angular eigenfrequency by the factor $2\pi$. Together, frequency and growth rate specify the mode's temporal evolution. Unlike the [local Alfvén continuum frequency](name:alfven_frequency), this quantity characterizes the specified linear MHD mode rather than a continuum branch evaluated on an individual flux surface. Sign convention: Positive when the temporal phase of the complex perturbation decreases with increasing time under the stated exponential convention.

Standard name: per_toroidal_mode_total_absorbed_wave_power_density
Definition (stored description): Volumetric rate of coherent-wave energy deposition into all plasma particle populations for each toroidal Fourier mode, resolved across a poloidal cross-section.

Documentation (stored): Mode-resolved absorbed wave power density is the rate at which energy is transferred directly from an individual toroidal wave harmonic to plasma particles per unit physical volume. It resolves the spatial distribution of absorption across a poloidal cross-section rather than averaging over a magnetic flux surface. For each toroidal harmonic, the absorbed power density is defined by $$ p_{\mathrm{abs},n_\phi} = \sum_s \frac{dE^{\mathrm{wave}}_{s,n_\phi}}{dt\,dV} $$ where $p_{\mathrm{abs},n_\phi}$ is the modal absorbed power density, $n_\phi$ is the integer toroidal Fourier mode number, $s$ indexes nonoverlapping plasma particle populations, $E^{\mathrm{wave}}_{s,n_\phi}$ is the energy transferred directly from that harmonic to population $s$, $t$ is time, and $V$ is physical volume. The population sum includes electrons, ions, and fast-particle populations without double counting. Unlike [fast-ion charge-state power density per toroidal mode](name:per_toroidal_mode_fast_ion_charge_state_power_density), it is not restricted to a particular species, charge state, or fast population. It excludes energy remaining in the wave fields, unabsorbed launched power, and subsequent collisional redistribution of deposited energy. The modal contribution is an absorbed-power contribution associated with a wave harmonic, not a complex Fourier coefficient of the power-density field itself. Summing over the complete toroidal mode set recovers [total absorbed wave power density](name:total_absorbed_wave_power_density): $p_{\mathrm{abs}} = \sum_{n_\phi} p_{\mathrm{abs},n_\phi}$, where $p_{\mathrm{abs}}$ is the mode-summed absorbed power density. Integrating each modal contribution over the plasma volume gives the corresponding [absorbed wave power per toroidal mode](name:per_toroidal_mode_total_absorbed_wave_power).
Assigned physics domain: waves

Standard name: power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination

Definition (stored description): Total power deposited on a divertor target by recombination processes, summing the plasma-ion and neutral-particle recombination channels at the plasma-material interface.

Documentation (stored): This quantity captures the combined recombination power delivered to a single divertor target, encompassing two physically distinct contributions: energy released when plasma ions recombine at or near the target surface (the plasma channel, quantified by plasma_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination) and energy deposited when neutral particles undergo recombination into lower-energy bound states at the material wall (the neutral channel, quantified by [neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination](name:neutral_power_at_divertor_target_due_to_recombination)). The total recombination power at the target decomposes additively: $$ P_{\rm rec,target} = P_{\rm rec,plasma} + P_{\rm rec,neutral} $$ where $P_{\rm rec,plasma}$ is the ion-recombination contribution and $P_{\rm rec,neutral}$ is the neutral-particle recombination contribution, both in W. This target-localized quantity is a spatial specialization of the volume-integrated [power_due_to_recombination](name:power_due_to_recombination), which integrates recombination power over the full plasma domain. In attached divertor operation, recombination power at the target is a minor fraction of the total heat load; in detached or high-recycling regimes, surface and volumetric recombination become significant energy sinks that reduce the conducted and convected flux reaching the target. It is inferred from edge plasma simulations or from particle flux measurements combined with surface energy-release models, and is non-negative by definition.

abla_R n_s = \hat{\mathbf{R}}\cdot

Definition (stored description): Real part of the first-order radial magnetic-vector-potential eigenfunction for a single toroidal mode in the vacuum region.

Documentation (stored): The quantity is the real radial projection of the first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region for one toroidal Fourier mode. The real part is defined relative to the phase reference of that complex eigenfunction. $$ A_{R,\mathrm{vac}}^{\mathrm{Re}} = \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}\right) $$ Here $A_{R,\mathrm{vac}}^{\mathrm{Re}}$ is the requested real radial component, $\widetilde{\mathbf{A}}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the complex first-order perturbed magnetic vector-potential eigenfunction in the vacuum region, $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the radial unit vector, and $\operatorname{Re}$ denotes the real-part operation. The radial direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The quantity applies outside the plasma and to one toroidal Fourier mode; it is not summed over modes. It excludes the plasma-region perturbation, the imaginary component, and the unreduced complex radial component. The [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic vector potential](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_vector_potential) is the full complex parent quantity, of which this entry is the real-part component. It is distinct from the [radial perturbed vacuum magnetic field](name:radial_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field), which is a magnetic-field perturbation rather than a vector potential. Sign convention: Positive when the real radial projection points toward increasing major radius $R$.

Standard name: radial_separatrix_distance_at_outboard_midplane

Definition (stored description): Signed major-radius separation from the separatrix after mapping a measurement position along its flux surface to the outboard midplane, with positive values in the scrape-off layer.

Documentation (stored): This quantity is the signed major-radius offset between a measurement position mapped along its magnetic flux surface to the outboard midplane and the separatrix at that locus. The defining relation is $$ \Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}} = R_{\mathrm{mapped}} - R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}} $$ where $\Delta R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the signed separation, $R_{\mathrm{mapped}}$ is the major radius of the mapped measurement position, and $R_{\mathrm{sep,mid}}$ is the major radius of the separatrix intersection at the outboard midplane. Both radii are coordinates in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The mapping preserves the magnetic flux label of the original measurement position. The result is a difference of major radii, not the [radial coordinate assigned to a flux surface](name:radial_coordinate_of_flux_surface), an unmapped local separation, or the shortest distance normal to the separatrix. It vanishes on the separatrix and is negative on the confined-plasma side. Sign convention: Positive when the mapped measurement position has a larger major radius than the separatrix at the outboard midplane, corresponding to the scrape-off-layer side. The low-field-side equatorial midplane: the point of maximum major radius on the flux surface in question. For a value at the separatrix intersection use outboard_midplane_separatrix. Where $R = \max_{S} R,\quad R > R_{\mathrm{axis}}$, $S$ is the magnetic flux surface the point lies on; $R_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is major radius of the magnetic axis.

Standard name: radius_of_poloidal_field_coil

Definition (stored description): Non-negative curvature radius of one arc-of-circle segment used to approximate the cross-sectional contour of a poloidal field coil. The contour lies in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, where R is major radius and Z is vertical height.

Documentation (stored): Radius of a poloidal-field-coil arc is the non-negative circle radius of a single circular segment of the coil cross-sectional contour, taken in a poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. The conductor or winding-pack boundary is approximated by connected circular arcs, and this quantity sets the local radius of curvature of one such arc. For a circular contour segment, the curvature radius $\rho$ (in m) is the inverse magnitude of the planar curvature $\kappa$ (in m$^{-1}$) of the boundary curve in the $(R, Z)$ cross-section: $$ \rho = \frac{1}{|\kappa|} $$ where a finite physical arc has $\rho > 0$, and as $\rho$ grows the segment approaches a straight line ($\kappa \to 0$). Each arc is anchored by a start point in the poloidal plane: its major-radius coordinate is given by major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil and its vertical coordinate by [height_of_poloidal_field_coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil); both together with $\rho$ are needed to locate and shape one arc, with the end of each arc coinciding with the start of the next. The value is determined from the designed circular-arc contour, from CAD geometry, or by fitting circular arcs to surveyed boundary points. Small radii represent tightly rounded corners and compact winding-pack features, while larger radii represent gently curved coil sides; the magnitude scales with coil aperture, winding-pack dimensions, and mechanical-clearance requirements. An analogous arc-of-circle convention applies to iron core segment boundaries via radius_of_iron_core_segment.

Standard name: right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field

Definition (stored description): Complex E-minus contribution of a coherent electromagnetic-wave electric field, transverse to the static magnetic field and retaining the amplitude and phase of its right-hand circular polarization.

Documentation (stored): The right-hand circularly polarized wave electric field is the E-minus polarization contribution of the complex [wave electric field](name:wave_electric_field), perpendicular to the local static magnetic field. It retains the local amplitude and phase of that circular-polarization contribution. Its vector contribution is defined by the circular-basis projection $$ \widetilde{\mathbf E}_{-}=\widetilde E_{-}\mathbf e_{-}=\mathbf e_{-}\left(\mathbf e_{-}^{*}\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf E}_{\mathrm{wave}}\right) $$ where $\widetilde{\mathbf E}_{-}$ is the right-hand circularly polarized vector contribution, $\widetilde E_{-}$ is its complex coefficient, $\widetilde{\mathbf E}_{\mathrm{wave}}$ is the wave-electric-field phasor, and the asterisk denotes complex conjugation. The circular basis vector is $\mathbf e_{-}=(\hat{\mathbf e}_1+i\hat{\mathbf e}_2)/\sqrt{2}$, where $i$ is the imaginary unit. The real unit vectors form a local right-handed orthonormal frame $(\hat{\mathbf e}_1,\hat{\mathbf e}_2,\hat{\mathbf b})$, with $\hat{\mathbf b}$ pointing along the static magnetic field and the first two directions perpendicular to it. With temporal dependence $e^{-i\omega t}$, where $\omega$ is the wave angular frequency and $t$ is time, this polarization rotates opposite to positive-ion gyromotion. The complementary [left-hand circularly polarized wave electric field](name:left_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field) co-rotates with positive ions. Handedness is defined relative to the static magnetic field, not the wave-propagation direction. This quantity includes only the right-hand transverse wave contribution; it excludes the parallel wave component and non-wave electric fields. It is local and is not restricted to a beam or ray path. The full complex contribution is distinct from its amplitude representation, which removes the coefficient's complex phase, and from its real and [imaginary quadratures](name:right_hand_circularly_polarized_wave_electric_field_imaginary_part), which separately retain phase-referenced parts of the same phasor.
Stored unit: V.m^-1

Standard name: spectral_photon_radiance
Definition (stored description): Spectral photon radiance is the directional photon arrival rate from plasma emission per projected area, viewing solid angle, and wavelength interval.

Documentation (stored): Spectral photon radiance describes the absolute photon-number brightness of plasma radiation along a specified viewing direction, resolved by wavelength. Its spectral dependence is expressed per wavelength interval, not per frequency or photon-energy interval. The defining differential relation is: $$ dN_{\gamma} = L_{\gamma}(\lambda)\,dt\,dA_{\perp}\,d\Omega\,d\lambda $$ where $N_{\gamma}$ is the number of photons crossing a collecting surface, $L_{\gamma}(\lambda)$ is the spectral photon radiance at wavelength $\lambda$, $t$ is time, $A_{\perp}$ is the collecting surface's projected area perpendicular to the ray direction, and $\Omega$ is the solid angle about that direction. The quantity includes the line and continuum contributions present at the specified wavelength without selecting a particular emitting species or radiation mechanism. It is not a local volumetric photon-production rate, an electromagnetic energy radiance, or a detector count rate. Integrating the contribution from an identified transition over its wavelength interval gives the [photon radiance at a spectral line](name:photon_radiance_at_spectral_line), rather than a wavelength-resolved radiance density. The [spectral bremsstrahlung photon radiance](name:spectral_bremsstrahlung_photon_radiance) is the contribution restricted to free-free emission.

Standard name: temperature_of_sensor
Definition (stored description): Thermodynamic temperature associated with a selected thermocouple sensor attached to a tokamak structural component.

Documentation (stored): This quantity is the absolute thermodynamic temperature associated with one selected sensor member, represented by the thermal state at its thermocouple junction. It characterizes the local thermal condition of the attached structural component at the sensor location. For a system in thermodynamic equilibrium, temperature is defined by $$ T = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial S}\right)_{V,N} $$ where $T$ is thermodynamic temperature, $U$ is internal energy, $S$ is entropy, $V$ is volume, and $N$ is the amount of material or particle number held fixed in the derivative. The quantity applies to the selected sensor member individually and is not a sum, average, or other aggregation over the sensor set. It denotes the sensor or junction thermal state associated with a structural component, not the temperature of a flowing coolant or of an entire plant connection. It is distinct from [coolant temperature at inlet](name:coolant_temperature_at_inlet), which describes fluid entering a cooling system. Object-specific quantities such as [temperature of a coil conductor](name:temperature_of_coil_conductor) and [temperature of a neutron detector](name:temperature_of_neutron_detector) apply the same thermodynamic concept to explicitly named hardware rather than to the generic sensor locus.

Standard name: thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket
Definition (stored description): Thermal power of the breeder blanket is the aggregate rate of energy deposition as heat in its breeding zone.

Documentation (stored): Thermal power of the breeder blanket is the incoming heat load deposited in its breeding zone. It denotes blanket-level heat input rather than heat extraction from an individual module. The defining energy-transfer rate is $$ P = \frac{dE_{\mathrm{dep}}}{dt} $$ where $P$ is the thermal power deposited in the breeder blanket, $E_{\mathrm{dep}}$ is the cumulative energy deposited there as heat, and $t$ is time. The quantity aggregates heat deposition at the blanket level without specifying a particular deposition mechanism or restricting deposition to the plasma-facing surface. Unlike [nuclear heating power of the breeder blanket](name:nuclear_heating_power_of_breeder_blanket), which isolates heat generation from neutron and photon interactions, it is not restricted to nuclear heating. The [net thermal power of a breeder blanket module](name:net_thermal_power_of_breeder_blanket_module) instead quantifies heat removal by that module's coolant. Incoming deposited power need not equal simultaneous coolant heat removal, since energy accumulation and other energy transfers also enter the blanket energy balance.

Standard name: toroidal_angle_of_poloidal_magnetic_field_probe
Definition (stored description): Signed azimuthal orientation angle of a poloidal magnetic-field probe’s sensitive-axis normal in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.

Documentation (stored): This quantity is the signed toroidal orientation of the sensitive-axis normal of a poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It measures the normal’s departure from the poloidal plane through the orientation of its horizontal projection. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the angle is defined by $$ \alpha_{\mathrm{tor}} = \operatorname{atan2}(n_\phi,n_R), \qquad n_R=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{R}}, \quad n_\phi=\mathbf{n}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} $$ where $\alpha_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal orientation angle, $\mathbf{n}$ is the probe’s sensitive-axis unit normal, $n_R$ and $n_\phi$ are its cylindrical radial and toroidal components, and $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ are the radial and toroidal unit vectors. Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; $\operatorname{atan2}$ returns the signed angle from the positive radial direction to the horizontal projection of $\mathbf{n}$. The quantity applies to the geometric orientation of each poloidal magnetic-field probe coil. It is not the local plasma magnetic field, a field component, or an angle averaged over probes, turns, or field samples. The angle determines how the probe’s sensitive direction is related to the local magnetic-field vector and therefore how the measured component is projected. The corresponding toroidal orientation for a toroidal probe is defined by [toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:toroidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe), while its independent poloidal tilt is represented by [poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe](name:poloidal_angle_of_toroidal_magnetic_field_probe). Sign convention: Positive when rotation from the positive radial direction toward the horizontal projection of the sensitive-axis normal is toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

Standard name: toroidal_parity
Definition (stored description): Orientation indicator equal to the sign of the toroidal magnetic-field component on a flux surface in local gyrokinetic geometry.

Documentation (stored): The toroidal magnetic-field sign specifies whether the equilibrium toroidal field component on a flux surface is directed along or opposite increasing toroidal angle in local gyrokinetic geometry. For a nonzero toroidal magnetic-field component, the orientation indicator is defined by $$ s_\phi = \operatorname{sgn}(B_\phi) = \frac{B_\phi}{|B_\phi|} $$ where $s_\phi$ is the orientation indicator, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component, and $\operatorname{sgn}$ is the sign function. The component is $B_\phi = \mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}$, where $\mathbf{B}$ is the equilibrium magnetic field and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle. The right-handed cylindrical frame is $(R,\phi,Z)$, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. As the toroidal member of [parity](name:parity), this quantity retains only field orientation and takes the values $+1$ or $-1$; the two-valued indicator is undefined when the toroidal component vanishes. It does not specify field strength, plasma-current direction, or the even or odd symmetry of a gyrokinetic perturbation. Sign convention: Positive when the toroidal magnetic-field component points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

Standard name: toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field

Definition (stored description): Toroidal magnetic field perturbation in the current-free vacuum surrounding the plasma, represented by a complex first-order eigenfunction for one toroidal Fourier mode.

Documentation (stored): Toroidal magnetic field perturbation is the toroidal component of the first-order [magnetic induction](name:magnetic_field) eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum surrounding the plasma for one toroidal Fourier mode in linear magnetohydrodynamics. It excludes the background equilibrium field. The component is defined by projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame: $$ \widetilde{\delta B}_{\mathrm{vac},\phi}=\widetilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_{\mathrm{vac}}\cdot\hat{\phi} $$ where $\widetilde{\delta B}_{\mathrm{vac},\phi}$ is the complex toroidal perturbation component, $\widetilde{\delta\mathbf{B}}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the parent [perturbed vacuum magnetic-field vector](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field), and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$. Here $R$ is distance from the symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height. This quantity retains both phase coefficients without selecting either one. Their relationship is $\widetilde{\delta B}_{\mathrm{vac},\phi}=B_{\phi,\mathrm{r}}+iB_{\phi,\mathrm{i}}$, where $B_{\phi,\mathrm{r}}$ is its [real part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part), $B_{\phi,\mathrm{i}}$ is its [imaginary part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part), and $i$ is the imaginary unit. These specialized forms select the in-phase and quadrature coefficients under the same Fourier-phase convention; neither alone is the full complex component or its magnitude. Together with the other spatial components, including the [poloidal component](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field), it describes the vector vacuum perturbation. It is a local toroidal projection, not the vector magnitude, a toroidal average, or a sum over toroidal modes. Sign convention: Positive when the physical magnetic-field perturbation has a component along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$, counter-clockwise when viewed from the positive $Z$ axis toward the horizontal plane.
Standard name: toroidal_reference_magnetic_field

Definition (stored description): Toroidal reference magnetic field is the signed toroidal component of the equilibrium magnetic field at the reference point whose major radius is the reference major radius, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame.

Documentation (stored): Toroidal reference magnetic field is the signed toroidal component of the equilibrium magnetic field at a specified reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The reference point has major radius equal to the [reference major radius](name:reference_major_radius). The defining projection is: $$ B_{\phi,\mathrm{ref}} = \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{eq}}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ref}}) \cdot \hat{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ref}}) $$ where $B_{\phi,\mathrm{ref}}$ is the toroidal reference magnetic field, $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is the equilibrium magnetic field, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ref}}=(R_{\mathrm{ref}},\phi_{\mathrm{ref}},Z_{\mathrm{ref}})$ is the full reference point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the reference major radius, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing $\phi$. For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the value is independent of $\phi_{\mathrm{ref}}$. This quantity is the reference-location specialization of [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field). It is distinct from [toroidal magnetic field at magnetic axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis), from the magnetic-field magnitude, and from [toroidal vacuum magnetic field](name:toroidal_vacuum_magnetic_field). Sign convention: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Standard name: tungsten_density
Definition (stored description): Number density of tungsten ions summed over all positive ionization states, excluding neutral tungsten, at a specified location or spatial average.

Documentation (stored): Tungsten-ion number density is the particle count per unit volume for all positively charged tungsten ions, with neutral tungsten excluded. It may denote a local value or a spatially averaged value over a defined domain. The charge-state-summed density is defined by $$ n_{\mathrm{W}} = \sum_{Z=1}^{74} n_{\mathrm{W}}^{Z+} $$ where $n_{\mathrm{W}}$ and $n_{\mathrm{W}}^{Z+}$ are number densities in m$^{-3}$, and $Z$ is the positive tungsten charge state. Specific instances include [volume-averaged tungsten density](name:volume_averaged_tungsten_density), [tungsten density at magnetic axis](name:tungsten_density_at_magnetic_axis), and [tungsten density at divertor target](name:tungsten_density_at_divertor_target); these differ by evaluation locus or averaging domain. Neutral tungsten is not included.
Standard name: y_major_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone
Definition (stored description): The signed y component of the unit vector along the major axis of an elliptic shatter cone is its projection in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.

Documentation (stored): The signed y component of the unit vector along the major axis of an elliptic shatter cone is the projection of that major-axis direction onto the $y$ basis direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. The major-axis direction is the orientation of the principal semiaxis of the cone's elliptic cross-section. The component is defined by $$ e_{\mathrm{maj},y} = \hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}} \cdot \hat{y} $$ where $e_{\mathrm{maj},y}$ is the y component of the shatter-cone major-axis unit vector, $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}}$ is the unit vector along the major axis of the elliptic shatter cone, and $\hat{y}$ is the y basis vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame. This quantity applies to the geometry of an elliptic shatter cone and to the major semiaxis orientation of its elliptic cross-section; its aggregation convention is none, because it is a single vector component rather than a sum or mean. It is distinct from the unsigned major-axis length, from the [y component of the shatter-cone direction unit vector](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), which describes the cone direction rather than the major-axis orientation, and from the [y component of the minor-axis unit vector](name:y_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), which refers to the orthogonal minor semiaxis. Together with the [x component](name:x_major_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone) and [z component](name:z_major_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), this quantity forms the Cartesian representation of $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}}$; the linked x and z components and $e_{\mathrm{maj},y}$ satisfy $(e_{\mathrm{maj},x})^2 + (e_{\mathrm{maj},y})^2 + (e_{\mathrm{maj},z})^2 = 1$, where $e_{\mathrm{maj},x}$ and $e_{\mathrm{maj},z}$ are the linked x and z components. The major-axis and minor-axis unit vectors jointly orient the elliptic cone and satisfy $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}} \cdot \hat{e}_{\mathrm{min}} = 0$, where $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{min}}$ is the minor-axis unit vector with [x](name:x_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), [y](name:y_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone), and [z](name:z_minor_axis_unit_vector_of_shatter_cone) components. Sign convention: Positive when $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{maj}}$ has a component in the $+\hat{y}$ direction of the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame.

Standard name: z_direction_unit_vector_of_camera
Definition (stored description): Signed Z-direction cosine of a camera’s viewing-direction unit vector in the right-handed Cartesian (x, y, z) frame.

Documentation (stored): The camera direction component along the Cartesian Z axis is the signed directional cosine of the camera’s viewing-direction unit vector. It specifies how strongly the viewing direction points along the positive or negative Z direction. The component is defined by $$ d_z = \mathbf{d} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}} $$ where $d_z$ is the Z component, $\mathbf{d}$ is the camera’s direction unit vector, and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the positive-Z basis vector of the right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame. This quantity applies to the viewing direction of an individual camera, with no spatial, population, or charge-state aggregation. It is a directional component rather than the camera position, the image-up orientation, or the magnitude of the direction vector. Together with the corresponding [x direction unit vector of the camera](name:x_direction_unit_vector_of_camera) and [y direction unit vector of the camera](name:y_direction_unit_vector_of_camera), it specifies the complete viewing-direction vector; the three components satisfy $d_x^2 + d_y^2 + d_z^2 = 1$, where $d_x$ and $d_y$ are the X and Y components of that same unit vector.
